content: Faecal incontinence is a challenging and distressing condition that carries significant social stigma. For some individuals, neither conservative management nor surgical interventions are sufficient to address the issue, necessitating the use of containment products such as anal plugs. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various types of anal plugs in managing faecal incontinence. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Register, which includes trials from multiple sources such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP). The search also included handsearching journals and conference proceedings, and contacting plug manufacturers for relevant trials. No restrictions were placed on language or other criteria. The review focused on randomised and quasi-randomised controlled trials, including crossover studies, that investigated the use of anal plugs for managing faecal incontinence. Participants included both children and adults with this condition. The interventions studied included any type of anal plug, with comparisons made to no treatment, conservative physical treatments, nutritional interventions, surgical options, pads, or other types and sizes of plugs. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the included studies and extracted relevant data. Authors of the included trials were contacted for clarification on methodological issues. The review included four studies with a total of 136 participants. Two studies compared the use of anal plugs to no plugs, one study compared two sizes of the same brand of plug, and one study compared two different brands of plugs. A significant dropout rate was observed across the studies, with 48 participants (35%) discontinuing participation before the studies concluded, for various reasons. This high dropout rate introduces potential bias into the findings. Despite these limitations, some participants who continued using anal plugs achieved a state of pseudo-continence, at least in the short term. In one study comparing two different types of plugs, polyurethane plugs were associated with less frequent plug loss and higher overall satisfaction compared to polyvinyl-alcohol plugs. The authors concluded that the available data were limited and incomplete, preventing a comprehensive evaluation of all pre-specified outcomes. As a result, only tentative conclusions could be drawn. The findings suggest that while anal plugs can be difficult for some individuals to tolerate, they may be effective in preventing incontinence for those who can tolerate them. Anal plugs may therefore serve as a useful option for a select group of individuals, either as a substitute for other management strategies or as an adjunctive treatment. The review also highlighted that the design and size of the plug can influence its performance, underscoring the importance of selecting the appropriate type of plug for each individual.
